messages.subject: position change in procrustes graphs
messages.body_plain:
Hello, I am carrying out a geometric morphometric analysis on Espeletia seeds and when I obtain the Procrustes graph for each species, I find that in some graphs the silhouette of the landmarks is oriented towards the left (upper part of the seed), and in others it is mirrored, towards the right.
Could this be an error?
Can the graphs be oriented in the same direction? If so, how could I orient them?

messages.subject: New phylogenetic comparative method for high-dimensional data
messages.subject_clean: New phylogenetic comparative method for high-dimensional data
messages.body_plain:
Colleagues,

I wish to alert you to a new paper of interest to morphometricians that wish to investigate macroevolutionary patterns in shape variation, and require phylogenetic comparative methods. The paper is currently in Early View at Methods in Ecology and Evolution (https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.14438).

In this paper, Mike Collyer and I describe a new method, E-PGLS: an extended phylogenetic least squares regression approach for the analysis of high-dimensional data. E-PGLS allows one to utilize more than one individual per species directly in the analysis, rather than relying on species means. The method has two primary purposes. First, it allows one to incorporate within-species variation in their phylogenetic comparative analyses of multivariate data. When used in this manner, it is equivalent to other methods for incorporating within-species variation (e.g., Felsenstein 2008).

Additionally, E-PGLS allows one to compare within-species trends across species while simultaneously accounting for phylogenetic non-independence. In this capacity, it is useful for determining whether intraspecific patterns, such as sexual dimorphism, allometry, population-level divergence, etc., differ across species, but does so in a phylogenetically-informed context (something inaccessible with current approaches).

Because morphometricians commonly have datasets comprising many individuals per species, and often wish to incorporate them when evaluating their evolutionary hypotheses, we hope that this new procedure assists you all in your analytical endeavors.

Presently the method is implemented in RRPP as `lm.rrpp.ws <http://lm.rrpp.ws>`. We are finishing the equivalent function for shape-specific data, to be included in geomorph, and will let you all know when it is ready for distribution.  In the meantime, we encourage you to read the paper and learn what E-PGLS provides.

Best,

Dean and Mike

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

https://faculty.sites.iastate.edu/dcadams/

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] position change in procrustes graphs
messages.body_plain:
Without knowing your particular dataset, I suspect that there is some symmetry in your data. That is, you may have some ‘right-handed’ and some ‘left-handed’ shaped seeds.

GM methods do not know whether this is a biological signal or whether they need to be reflected.  That is something the user needs to investigate. The functions in geomorph will not automatically reflect objects, as we cannot assume whether this is a biological difference or a user-input issue.

If you have such reflections you can reflect them using ‘rotate.coords’ prior to your GPA. The help file provides examples.

Dean

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

messages.subject: new versions of geomorph and RRPP available on CRAN
messages.subject_clean: new versions of geomorph and RRPP available on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
Colleagues,

I’m pleased to announce the release of new versions of both geomorph (vsn. 4.0.9) and RRPP (vsn. 2.0.4), which are available on CRAN.  There are two new and important functions that are included in these updates:

1: The function ‘physignal.eigen’ is a new approach that allows one to interrogate dimensions of phylogenetic signal in multivariate datasets. In particular, the method allows one to investigate the degree to which phylogenetic signal is concentrated in one or a few dimensions of shape space, which is likely common in empirical systems. The approach was recently described in Mitteroecker, Collyer, and Adams 2024. https://doi.org/10.1093/sysbio/syae035

2: The function ‘extended.pgls’ is a novel phylogenetic comparative method for multivariate phenotypes. The method has two primary applications. First, it allows users to include more than one individual per species in the analysis (as opposed to using species means). Second, it enables the ability to compare within-species trends across species while simultaneously accounting for phylogenetic non-independence (e.g., compare the degree of sexual dimorphism across taxa while conditioning those patterns on the phylogeny). The method was recently described in Adams and Collyer 2024: https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.14438

To use these new approaches, please be sure to install both the latest RRPP and the latest geomorph.

We hope you find the new procedures useful for furthering your research endeavors.

Best,

Dean (on behalf of the geomorph team).

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

messages.subject: Questions on warping meshes & plotting landmarks
messages.subject_clean: Questions on warping meshes & plotting landmarks
messages.body_plain:
Hi geomorph community,

I'm working on visualization of my brain shape data, and I have questions around the (1) plotReftoTarget function and (2) plotspec. For my project, I'm examining variation in brain shape among mustelid (badger/weasel/otter) species.

(1) I'm using plotReftoTarget to predict the shapes at the PC extremes. When considering the reference specimen, is it more appropriate to use the mean shape estimated from all the individual specimens or from species averages? There is a notable difference in the result, and surface meshes using the mean shape of all the individuals in the dataset (attachment: PC1...INDMEAN) look more like what I expected given the point and vector plots. I presume this discrepancy is related to the species mean being an average of an [species] average?

Also, I did check the scaling, though I'm unsure how to interpret/correct for this difference.
> range(gvitatta.ply$vb[1:3]) [1] -1.277344 1047.774780 > range(gvitatta.coords) [1] -54.59414 1064.74500

Tangentially related -- is there a way to move the "light source?" I did not change anything in my code other than the reference specimen, and the lighting has shifted. The plot is well-lit dorsally but not laterally or posteriorly.

(2) Re: plotspec - I have both curve and surface semilandmarks. Is there any way to delineate and plot the curve SLs in a different color alongside the fixed landmarks?

Thank you for your time, and I look forward to your advice and insights.

All the best,
Ani

Ani,

For visualizing deformations it is generally advised to use the overall mean of the dataset as the ‘reference’. So from your question that would mean the mean of the individuals, which is the consensus from the GPA.

Re lighting: Not sure on this one: geomorph does nothing regarding lighting of the surfaces.

Point colors: One could in theory obtain the output object, recolor manually, and then plot it.

Dean

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Questions on warping meshes & plotting landmarks
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Questions on warping meshes & plotting landmarks
messages.body_plain:
Dear Ani,

>
> (2) Re: plotspec - I have both curve and surface semilandmarks. Is there any way to delineate and plot the curve SLs in a different color alongside the fixed landmarks?

To answer your question most philosophically, there is always a way to plot what you want in R, as long as you are comfortable with R graphics.  But if you meant is there a way to manipulate geomorph functions without having to write complicated r scripts for graphics, then the answer is, “maybe”.

For example, one could do something like this:

> library(geomorph)
> data("pupfish")
> plotAllSpecimens(pupfish$coords, plot_param = list(pt.bg <http://pt.bg> = c(rep(1, 20), rep(2, 36)), mean.bg <http://mean.bg> = c(rep(1, 20), rep(2, 36))))

You could do something similar making sure to match colors with landmark numbers (the example above was simplistic and sloppy).  The plotAllSpecimens function is useful for quick plotting but maybe not as elegant as “do it yourself” plotting (because it lacks some capability of changing plotting parameters).  If you want the most control over your plots, there simply is no substitute for R graphics skill  For example, this is what I might do instead of above.

> library(geomorph)
> data("pupfish")
>
> plot(pupfish$coords[,,1],
+      type = "n",
+      asp = 1,
+      xlim = c(-0.25, 0.25),
+      ylim = c(-0.1, 0.1),
+      xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
+      xlab = "", ylab = "",
+      bty = "n")
>
> for(i in 1:length(pupfish$CS)) {
+   points(pupfish$coords[,, i],
+        pch = 16,
+        col = c(rep(1, 20), rep(2, 36)),
+        cex = c(rep(1, 20), rep(0.5, 36))
+        )
+ }
> points(mshape(pupfish$coords),
+        pch = 16, col = “gray”, cex = 0.6)

The point of this is that you can used canned functions with some capability of manipulating plot parameters or you can take complete control of the plot parameters.  Either way, yes you can change landmark colors based on type of landmark.

Best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
It is harder to control low-level openGL features like lighting and shading in R. If you want to have better visualization of meshes, use a proper 3D rendering program like 3D Slicer that supports many different shading and surface rendering techniques. You can do couple things:
1. You can export your deformed meshes (extremes) as PlYs and render them in 3D Slicer
2 If you want more interactivity, and possibly want to make animations of transformation, you can export your geomorph results to SlicerMorph, and then use the GPA module in SlicerMorph to do the visualizations. We have a function called geomorph2slicermorph2 to do that. There is some documentation of this, but feel free to reach out if it is not clear enough.
https://github.com/SlicerMorph/SlicerMorphR?tab=readme-ov-file#how-to-run-a-geomorph-analysis-with-slicermorph-data-and-get-the-results-back-into-slicermorph-for-visualization

I'm looking for a paper/s on effects of increasing subsampling of semilandmarks on ability to distinguish groups or some other metric of "fit". I seem to recall something like that from Mike on fish outlines but can't find it now. Essentially I am wondering if one were to plot # of landmarks on x axis and some other metric of accuracy/precision or likewise on the y, what would that be? Procrustes variance? In our case we are dealing with sliding semilandmarks across scapulae of hominids.

Thanks for any leads,
Christy
